judge.label: LLM rubric score, fresh-context judge, self-assessed — not human QA.
judge.independence_caveat: This judge is a different model family and a fresh context: it saw only the judge prompt, the rubric and the lesson. It did not direct the project and did not author anything in it. It is still a language model scoring a language model's output, so the label applies: not human QA.

notes.objective_alignment: Every block serves PRV-01, but coverage is uneven: need-to-know, collection minimisation, and data-subject requests appear only as takeaway bullets, never taught in a dedicated block — yet KC-02 then tests DSR handling. The takeaways block is doing teaching work, not summarising.
notes.level_fidelity: L1 (recognise/define) and L2 (decide/apply) are genuinely what the learner experiences, and the definition cards are real term cards, not lists with borders. Held at 4 because the L1 takeaways smuggle three untaught concepts into the level, blurring what L1 actually covers before L2 applies them.

verdict_notes: Strong, authentic lesson: the worked example's steps each name the judgement and what would change it, both knowledge checks draw distractors from real misconceptions (name-equals-personal, internal-equals-not-personal, helpful-equals-compliant) with feedback that explains why, and the autocomplete/same-name/5pm scenario is instantly recognisable with real friction. The Arabic reads as written in Arabic — idiomatic, correct legal-adjacent terminology, no English word order — and the licensed-content constraint is turned into a teaching point via regime-neutral phrasing. The one soft spot is structural: minimisation, need-to-know, and data-subject requests live only in the takeaway list, so the first real teaching of DSR handling happens in KC-02's feedback rather than in a block.
